## Part 1: Restaurant Health Inspections (25 points)

The first dataset contains restaurant health inspection scores from Montgomery County. Load the data from: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dwillis/jour405/refs/heads/main/data/montco_inspections.csv`

The dataset includes the name of the establishment, the number of points for critical and non-critical areas, the total points, maximum points possible, the compliance score, and the grade.

### Task 1: Read the data (2 points)

```{r}
restaurant_inspection <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dwillis/jour405/refs/heads/main/data/montco_inspections.csv")
```

### Task 2: Calculate the mean, standard deviation, minimum, and maximum of compliance scores. Save the results in a new dataframe called `compliance_stats`. (6 points)

```{r}
compliance_stats <- restaurant_inspection |> summarize(mean = mean(compliance_score), sd = sd(compliance_score), min = min(compliance_score), max = max(compliance_score))
```

### Task 3: Create a histogram of the compliance scores with a vertical line showing the mean. Include a headline and label the x and y axes. (8 points)

```{r}
restaurant_inspection |> 
  ggplot() + 
  geom_histogram(aes(x = compliance_score), binwidth = 2) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = mean(compliance_score)), color = "red", linetype = "dashed", size = 1) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = mean(compliance_score) - sd(compliance_score)), color = "blue", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = mean(compliance_score) + sd(compliance_score)), color = "blue", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1)
  labs(
    title = "Montgomery County Restaurant Compliance Scores",
    x = "Compliance Score",
    y = "Count")
```

### Task 4: Write 2–3 sentences interpreting what the standard deviation and histogram tell us about the distribution of compliance scores. What would be newsworthy about this distribution? What's the story here? (9 points)

The mean compliance score is 96.31 with the largest count of scores coming in at 100. The histogram is skewed left with more measurements above the mean than below it. The standard deviation gives journalists a reasonable range that helps them determine what certain measurements mean in relation to the mean. The newsworthiness of this story might be in how many Montgomery County restaurants received such high scores. There may be some room for questioning considering so many restaurants were given 100's and A-grades.

## Part 2: Daily Transit Ridership — Z-Scores (30 points)

Your editor wants you to identify unusual days in WMATA's daily ridership data that might be worth investigating as story leads. The dataset contains daily bus and rail totals, along with the day of the week. Load the data from: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dwillis/jour405/refs/heads/main/data/wmata_daily.csv`

### Task 5: Load the WMATA ridership data. (2 points)

```{r}
wmata_daily_ridership <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dwillis/jour405/refs/heads/main/data/wmata_daily.csv")
```

### Task 6: Using `mutate()`, add a column called `rail_zscore` that is the z-score for rail ridership, calculated using the overall mean and standard deviation of all days. Save the result as `wmata_zscores`. (7 points)

```{r}
wmata_zscores <- wmata_daily_ridership |> mutate(rail_zscore=(total - mean(total)) / sd(total))
```

### Task 7: Rail ridership varies a lot by day of the week. Using `group_by()` and `mutate()`, add a column called `weekday_zscore` that calculates each day's rail z-score relative to other days with the same `weekday` (for example, a Sunday compared to other Sundays). Remember to `ungroup()` and save the result back to `wmata_zscores`. (8 points)

```{r}
weekday_zscore <- wmata_zscores |> 
  group_by(weekday) |>
  mutate (
     z_score = (total - mean(total)) / sd(total)
  )
```

### Task 8: Filter for days where the absolute value of `rail_zscore` is greater than 2, and separately for days where the absolute value of `weekday_zscore` is greater than 2. Arrange each so the most extreme days appear first. How many unusual days does each method find? (5 points)

```{r}
unusual_days <- wmata_zscores |>
  filter(abs(rail_zscore) > 2) |>
  arrange(desc(abs(rail_zscore)))

unusual_weekdays <- weekday_zscore |>
  filter(abs(z_score) > 2) |>
  arrange(desc(abs(z_score)))
```

**How many unusual days does each method find?**

There are 10 days found in the filter for overall rail z-scores.

There are 33 days found in the filter for overall weekday z-scores.


### Task 9: Write 2–3 sentences: How do the two lists of unusual days differ, and what story leads does each suggest? (8 points)

The size and variety of the lists differ. Many of the days in the overall rail z-score filter come in January, which could suggest a potential lead about why people ride the rail more in January or in the cold. That appears consistent with the weekday z-score filter, which shows the highest z-scores in the months of January and December. Actually, the third-highest z-score on the list is December 25th, which could garner a story lead.

## Part 3: Maryland Car Theft Rates (25 points)

Your editor has assigned you a story about car thefts in Maryland and wants you to find out which counties have the highest rates and which saw the biggest changes. The dataset contains car theft counts for Maryland counties in 2023 and 2024 along with population figures. Load the data from: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dwillis/jour405/refs/heads/main/data/md_car_thefts.csv`

### Task 10: Load the car thefts data. (2 points)

```{r}
md_car_thefts <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dwillis/jour405/refs/heads/main/data/md_car_thefts.csv")
```

### Task 11: Using `mutate()`, add two columns: `theft_rate`, the 2024 car theft rate per 10,000 residents, and `pct_change`, the percent change in thefts from 2023 to 2024. Save the result back to `md_car_thefts`. (10 points)

```{r}
md_car_change <- md_car_thefts |> mutate(theft_rate = (thefts_2024 / population) * 10000, pct_change = (thefts_2024 - thefts_2023)/(thefts_2023))
```


### Task 12: Show the five counties with the highest 2024 theft rate, the five with the largest percent increase, and the five with the largest percent decrease. (5 points)

```{r}
Highest 2024 theft rate:
  Baltimore City: 77.03
  Prince George's County: 72.52
  Baltimore County: 25.93
  Howard County: 23.91
  Anne Arundel County: 22.38
  
Largest Percent Increase:
  Allegany County: 37.14%
  Garrett County: 28.57%
  Queen Anne's County: 26.67%
  Anne Arundel County: 24.17%
  Cecil County: 18.00%
  
Largest Percent Decrease:
  Dorchester County: 52.17%
  Somerset County: 52.00%
  Baltimore City: 38.71%
  Carroll County: 29.58%
  Kent County: 27.27%
```

### Task 13: Write 2–3 sentences describing what these calculations reveal about car thefts in Maryland. What is the lede of a story based on your findings? (8 points)

One of the biggest revelations from this data set is that Baltimore City fostered a 38.71% decrease in theft from 2023 to 2024. That is significant considering it ranked third-highest among Maryland cities even though Baltimore has one of the largest populations among the group. The data also reveals that theft rates are higher in more populated areas. Four of the five cities with the highest theft rates are also in the top five for total population.

The lede of a story about Baltimore City may look something like this: "Despite maintaining the highest theft rate among Maryland cities, Baltimore City saw a 38.7% decrease in theft from 2023 to 2024, according to recent statistics."

## Part 4: Data Analysis Scenario (20 points)

A county parks department releases data showing that its 12 community swimming pools average 187 visitors per day during the summer season, with a standard deviation of 42 visitors across the pools' average daily attendance. Your editor suspects that a handful of pools are dramatically underperforming and wants a story. You also learn that the department's figures are based on a random sample of 60 days per pool rather than a complete count.

Write 4–5 sentences for each of the following questions:

### Question A: How would you use descriptive statistics and z-scores to identify which pools are genuinely underperforming, and why is that more useful than simply ranking pools by raw attendance? (10 points)

A z-score is a measure of how many standard deviations a measurement is from the mean. That statistic gives journalists an accurate representation of data in relation to the average of a data set. Calculating averages, z-scores, and standard deviations give you more of an accurate representation because they show the rates of which people are attending the pools. Raw attendance numbers may not tell the whole story, especially considering the data is a random sample of 60 days per pool. What if certain pools simply have more people on some of those 60 days? Statistics collect that raw data and turn it into something with significance in relation to the entire data set.


### Question B: The department collected its attendance figures using a random sample of 60 days per pool rather than tracking every day. What questions would you ask about the sample before relying on these figures for a story? What concerns would you raise in your story? (10 points)

I would ask the following questions:

Can a list of the days sampled be provided?
Can data from more days be acquired for a larger sample size?
Were the days the same for every pool?
Are there monthly statistics available?
What prevented pools from tracking attendance statistics everyday? The three summer months (June, July, and August) last roughly 90 days, so why were pools only able to track 60?

Potential concerns:

In my story, I would potentially bring up which pools are averaging more attendance while potentially giving reasons as to why. I would point out that the data was taken at random from a 60-day sample, so that the audience knows the context. I would potentially give factors as to why certain days may not garner strong performances for certain pools.
